title: Valerian Root and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Mix? Risks and Timing
excerpt: Can you take valerian root with alcohol? How the herbal sleep aid and alcohol stack in the brain, how long to wait, the apigenin sleep-stack question, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you take valerian root with alcohol? How the two stack as sedatives, how long to wait, apigenin and sleep stacks, and warning signs that need help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's best not to take valerian root and alcohol together. Valerian is a mild herbal sedative, and alcohol is a depressant. Both appear to work partly through the same calming system in the brain (the GABA system), so taking them at the same time can stack their effects: more drowsiness, slower reactions, and worse coordination than you'd get from either one alone. For a healthy adult, one valerian capsule after a single glass of wine is unlikely to be dangerous. A large dose of valerian on top of a heavy night of drinking, or valerian mixed with alcohol *and* a sleeping pill or anxiety medicine, is a genuinely risky combination.

**The quick rules:** Don't use valerian as a way to "come down" or fall asleep after drinking. If you've been drinking, wait until you're sober before taking valerian, and if you've taken valerian, skip alcohol for the rest of the night. Never drive after either. If you take prescription sleep, anxiety, pain, or seizure medicines, have liver disease, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or drink most days, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using valerian at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before using valerian if** you take any medicine that makes you drowsy (benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, opioids, gabapentin, some antidepressants, sedating antihistamines), you have liver disease, you're pregnant or breastfeeding, or you have surgery coming up. **Get medical help right away if** someone who mixed valerian and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, vomiting while very drowsy, or confused, or if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs after using valerian. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Valerian Root Actually Is

Valerian (*Valeriana officinalis*) is a flowering plant native to Europe and parts of Asia. The flowers smell sweet, but the part used in supplements is the root, which smells famously bad. Most people compare it to old socks or strong cheese. That smell comes from isovaleric acid and related compounds that form as the dried root ages.

People have used valerian as a calming herb since ancient Greece and Rome, and it's still one of the best-selling herbal sleep aids in Europe and the United States. You'll find it in several forms:

- **Capsules and tablets.** Usually a dried root extract, often in the range of a few hundred milligrams per serving.
- **Teas.** Dried root steeped in hot water, often blended with chamomile, lemon balm, or hops.
- **Tinctures.** Liquid extracts taken as drops. **Many valerian tinctures are made with alcohol**, so check the label if you're trying to avoid it entirely. The amount per dose is small, but it's worth knowing.
- **Combination "sleep" blends.** Valerian mixed with melatonin, magnesium, L-theanine, hops, passionflower, or chamomile. These are common, and they matter for this topic because each extra calming ingredient adds to the stack.

The compounds most often linked to valerian's effects are **valerenic acid** and a group called **valepotriates**, along with various other plant chemicals. The amount of each can vary a lot from product to product, which is one reason study results on valerian have been inconsistent.

## How Valerian Works in Your Brain

Your brain has a built-in braking system. The main "brake" chemical is GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). When GABA attaches to its receptors, especially the type called **GABA-A**, nerve cells become less likely to fire. The result is a calmer, sleepier, less alert state.

Lab research suggests valerenic acid interacts with GABA-A receptors and makes them respond more strongly to GABA. In other words, it presses gently on the same brake. Other valerian compounds have been studied for effects on adenosine receptors (the "sleep pressure" system that caffeine blocks) and serotonin receptors, though that research is mostly early and lab-based.

The important part for this article: valerian's calming effect is generally mild. It's nowhere near as strong as a prescription sedative. But "mild" depends on what else is pressing on the brake at the same time.

## How Alcohol Works on the Same System

Alcohol also boosts GABA-A activity, which is a big part of why a couple of drinks make you feel relaxed and why more drinks make you sleepy, clumsy, and slow to react. At the same time, alcohol dampens glutamate, the brain's main "go" signal. Our guide to [alcohol and GABA](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-gaba) explains this in more detail.

So when you combine the two, you have two substances leaning on the same brake. That's the core of the interaction. It isn't a chemical reaction between valerian and alcohol in your stomach. It's an **additive effect on your nervous system**: each one adds its own push toward sedation.

## What Happens When You Mix Valerian and Alcohol

Direct human research on valerian combined with alcohol is thin. There aren't large, modern trials that tell us exactly how much extra impairment to expect at a given dose. What we do have is a clear understanding of how both substances act, consistent safety guidance, and the general rule that applies to all sedatives: they add up.

Here's what that tends to look like in practice:

### More drowsiness than you planned for

The most likely effect is simply feeling much sleepier, sooner. For some people that sounds like the goal. The problem is that alcohol-driven sleep is poor-quality sleep (more on that below), and heavy sedation makes it harder to wake up if something is wrong, like feeling sick in the night.

### Slower reactions and worse coordination

Both substances slow reaction time and judgment. Combined, you may be more unsteady on your feet than you'd expect from the number of drinks you had. That raises the risk of falls, especially on stairs or in the dark, and it makes driving, cycling, or operating anything dangerous a clear no.

### A heavier next morning

Valerian can leave some people groggy the next day, particularly at higher doses. Add that to a hangover and you can wake up feeling foggy, slow, and unrested. Some people report a "valerian hangover" on its own; stacked with alcohol it tends to blur into a general fog.

### Higher risk with bigger doses and more ingredients

The risk scales with three things: how much you drank, how much valerian you took, and what else is in the mix. A single capsule of plain valerian after one drink is a very different situation from a "maximum strength" sleep blend after six drinks, or valerian plus alcohol plus a prescription sleeping pill. The more sedatives involved, the more you're moving toward dangerous territory, where breathing can slow and a person can be hard to wake.

### What about your liver?

Valerian is processed by the liver, and alcohol puts its own load on the liver too. Liver injury from valerian appears to be rare. There have been case reports of liver problems in people taking valerian, though many involved multi-ingredient products, which makes it hard to say which ingredient was responsible. The US National Institutes of Health's LiverTox database includes valerian among herbal products with reported liver injury. For an occasional social drinker using valerian now and then, this isn't the main concern. For someone who drinks heavily most days or already has liver problems, it's another reason to check with a doctor first.

## Can You Take Valerian After Drinking to Help You Sleep?

This is the question most people are really asking. You've had a few drinks, it's late, and you know from experience that you'll fall asleep fine but wake up at 3 a.m. with your heart pounding and your mind racing. Can valerian smooth that out?

The answer is: **it's not a good idea, and it probably won't fix the problem you're trying to fix.**

Here's why. Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster, but as your body clears it during the night, you get a rebound. Your sleep becomes lighter and more broken, REM sleep is disrupted, and many people wake up too early feeling wired. Our article on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers this in depth.

Valerian doesn't reverse that rebound. If you take it while alcohol is still in your system, you're mostly adding sedation at the front of the night, which is exactly when you need it least, and the 3 a.m. rebound still comes. You also take on the stacking risk described above.

If you want to sleep better after a night out, the steps with the best support are simple:

1. **Stop drinking a couple of hours or more before bed.** This gives your body time to clear some of the alcohol before you try to sleep.
2. **Drink water and eat something.** Going to bed dehydrated and on an empty stomach makes the night rougher.
3. **Keep the room cool and dark**, and skip screens if you can.
4. **Accept a slightly worse night** rather than trying to force sleep with another sedative.

If you regularly reach for something to help you sleep after drinking, that's useful information. It may be worth cutting back on how much or how late you drink, and it's a reasonable thing to raise with your doctor. For more context, see [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) and then keeps you awake.

## How Long to Wait Between Valerian and Alcohol

There's no official waiting time on valerian labels, and research doesn't give a precise number. Here are sensible, cautious guidelines:

- **If you've been drinking:** wait until you're fully sober before taking valerian. A practical rule is to skip valerian on any night you've had more than a drink or two. Your liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot from person to person.
- **If you've taken valerian:** don't start drinking later that evening. Valerian's noticeable effects usually wear off within several hours, but how long depends on the dose, the product, and your own body. Treat the rest of the night as a no-alcohol night.
- **If you take valerian every night for sleep:** have an honest conversation with your doctor or pharmacist about how alcohol fits into that routine. On drinking nights, the simplest choice is to skip the valerian.

## Does Valerian Help With a Hangover?

There is no good evidence that valerian helps with a hangover. It isn't designed to, and it doesn't address the main drivers of hangover symptoms, like dehydration, inflammation, poor sleep, low blood sugar, and the breakdown products of alcohol.

Some people find valerian tea calming the next day, especially if they feel anxious and on edge ("hangxiety"). A warm, caffeine-free tea can feel soothing, and there's nothing wrong with that once the alcohol has cleared. Just don't expect it to treat the hangover itself. If you're interested in gentle drinks for the morning after, our guide to the [best tea for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-tea-for-hangover) covers the options honestly.

For the hangover itself, the basics still win: water, electrolytes, food, rest, and time.

## Does Valerian Actually Work for Sleep?

It's worth being honest about this, because it changes the risk-benefit picture.

The research on valerian for sleep is mixed. Some small studies have found modest improvements in how quickly people fall asleep or how well they feel they slept. Others have found no meaningful difference compared with a placebo. Reviews of the evidence have often concluded that the results are inconsistent and that many studies were small or used very different products and doses. The US Office of Dietary Supplements describes the evidence as inconclusive, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline on treating chronic insomnia suggested that doctors *not* use valerian, because the benefit looked small and uncertain.

Some research suggests valerian, if it helps at all, may work better with regular use over a couple of weeks rather than as a one-off dose. That's another reason taking it once after a night of drinking is unlikely to do much.

None of this means valerian is useless for everyone. Some people find it helpful, and for a healthy adult it's generally well tolerated in the short term. But when the expected benefit is modest, it's even harder to justify the added risk of combining it with alcohol.

## Valerian, Apigenin, and Alcohol: The "Sleep Stack" Question

A lot of people searching for valerian and alcohol are actually using a **sleep stack**: a combination of supplements taken together at night. Popular versions often include valerian, **apigenin**, magnesium, L-theanine, melatonin, or glycine. Apigenin in particular has become popular after being recommended in sleep and wellness podcasts.

### What apigenin is

Apigenin is a flavonoid, a plant compound found in chamomile, parsley, celery, and some other herbs and vegetables. Chamomile tea is the most familiar source. As a supplement, it's usually sold in doses far higher than you'd get from a cup of tea.

In lab and animal studies, apigenin has been shown to interact with the GABA-A receptor at the same site that benzodiazepine drugs use, though much more weakly. Human evidence for apigenin on its own as a sleep aid is very limited. Most of what people cite comes from chamomile studies, which have shown mixed and generally modest effects.

### Can you take apigenin with alcohol?

The same logic applies as with valerian. Apigenin seems to be a mild calming compound that may touch the GABA system, and alcohol leans heavily on that same system. There's no good research on the combination in people, and no evidence that apigenin protects against alcohol's effects on sleep. The cautious approach is not to take it while alcohol is still in your system.

On its own, apigenin is probably a milder concern than valerian. The bigger issue is **the stack as a whole**. Each ingredient might be gentle, but valerian plus apigenin plus magnesium plus melatonin plus several drinks is a lot of calming input arriving at once. If one product or one ingredient makes you noticeably drowsy, that effect can grow when you add alcohol.

### A safer way to handle a sleep stack on drinking nights

- **Skip the stack on nights you drink.** It's the simplest rule and costs you very little.
- **If you only drank one drink early in the evening**, and you're used to your stack, the risk is lower, but consider leaving out the most sedating ingredients (valerian and melatonin are the usual ones).
- **Read every label.** Some blends contain several sedating herbs in one capsule, and some liquid sleep products contain alcohol.
- **Don't add a sleeping pill or sedating antihistamine on top.** Products like ZzzQuil or Benadryl are their own strong sedatives. See our guide on [ZzzQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/zzzquil-and-alcohol), and our [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) overview for every type of sleep product.

For individual stack ingredients, we have separate guides on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol), [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol), and [L-theanine and alcohol](/never-hungover/l-theanine-and-alcohol).

## Valerian Compared With Other Sleep Aids and Alcohol

Here's a rough guide to how valerian stacks up against other things people commonly combine with alcohol. "Concern level" refers to mixing each with alcohol, not to using it alone.

| Product | How it calms you | Concern level when mixed with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Valerian root | Mild GABA-A effect | Moderate: additive drowsiness, worse with big doses or blends |
| Apigenin / chamomile | Weak GABA-A effect | Low to moderate: mild on its own, adds up in stacks |
| Melatonin | Signals "night" to body clock | Low to moderate: drowsiness, and alcohol blunts its usefulness |
| L-theanine | Calming amino acid from tea | Low: generally mild |
| Kava | Kavalactones, GABA-related | High: strong additive sedation plus liver concerns |
| Sedating antihistamines (Benadryl, ZzzQuil) | Block histamine in brain | High: strong drowsiness and impairment |
| Prescription sleep or anxiety drugs | Strong GABA-A effects | Very high: talk to your doctor; can be dangerous |

If you're curious how the stronger options compare, see our guides to [kava and alcohol](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol), [trazodone and alcohol](/never-hungover/trazodone-and-alcohol), and [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol).

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

Some people should avoid combining valerian and alcohol entirely, and should talk to a doctor before using valerian at all:

- **People taking prescription sedatives.** This includes benzodiazepines (like Xanax, Valium, Ativan), sleeping pills (like Ambien), opioid pain medicines, gabapentin or pregabalin, barbiturates, and some antidepressants and antipsychotics. Valerian can add to their effects, and alcohol makes it worse. Our [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) guide covers one common example.
- **People with liver disease** or a history of high liver enzymes.
- **People who drink heavily most days.** Regular heavy drinking changes how your body handles sedatives and strains the liver.
- **Pregnant or breastfeeding people.** There isn't enough safety data on valerian in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
- **Children.** Valerian isn't recommended for young children without a doctor's guidance.
- **Anyone with surgery coming up.** Valerian may interact with anesthesia. Many surgeons and anesthesiologists ask patients to stop herbal supplements, including valerian, ahead of surgery, so tell your surgical team you use it.
- **Older adults.** Sensitivity to sedatives often goes up with age, and so does the risk of falls.

## Side Effects of Valerian on Its Own

Even without alcohol, valerian can cause side effects in some people. They're usually mild:

- Headache
- Dizziness
- Upset stomach
- Next-day grogginess or a "hungover" feeling
- Vivid dreams
- In a small number of people, feeling restless or more alert instead of calm

There have also been reports of withdrawal-like symptoms, such as anxiety and poor sleep, in people who stopped valerian suddenly after taking high doses for a long time. If you've used it nightly for months, it's reasonable to taper down rather than stop abruptly, and to check with your doctor.

## When to Get Medical Help

Most of the time, an evening of valerian and a couple of drinks will mean a heavy, groggy night and nothing worse. But mixing sedatives can occasionally become an emergency, especially with larger amounts of alcohol or additional medicines.

**Call 911 or get emergency help if someone:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing slowly (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or with long pauses
- Is vomiting while very drowsy or semi-conscious
- Has bluish or pale, clammy skin
- Is confused, has a seizure, or has a very low body temperature

While you wait for help, don't leave them alone, keep them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and don't try to "sleep it off" for them. These are also signs of alcohol poisoning, which can happen without any valerian at all.

**See a doctor soon if** you notice yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, ongoing nausea, or pain under your right ribs after using valerian, especially if you also drink regularly.

**If you notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or strong anxiety when you go without alcohol**, talk to a doctor. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous, and valerian is not a treatment for it. There are safe, effective medical options.

## A Better Approach for Sleep and the Morning After

If you're looking up valerian and alcohol, you probably care about two things: sleeping well after a night out and feeling okay the next morning. Here's what has the most support:

- **Drink less and finish earlier.** The single biggest improvement to post-drinking sleep comes from cutting the amount and stopping well before bed.
- **Alternate alcoholic drinks with water**, and eat a proper meal before or while drinking.
- **Save your sleep supplements for alcohol-free nights**, where they have a cleaner shot at helping and no stacking risk.
- **Build good sleep habits** on regular nights: consistent bedtimes, a cool dark room, and less late caffeine.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through these steps in more detail.

Some people also add a supplement aimed at the drinking itself rather than at sleep. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. A well-known 2012 study in rats found DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and appeared to act on the GABA-A receptor in a way that countered alcohol's effects. Most of the evidence so far comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. DHM is not a sleep aid, it isn't a substitute for drinking less, and there is no good evidence about combining it with valerian, so don't treat it as a reason to mix valerian and alcohol. If you want to try DHM on nights you drink, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers safety with other supplements and medicines.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you take valerian root with alcohol?**

It's best not to. Valerian and alcohol both calm the brain through the GABA system, so together they can make you more drowsy and impaired than either alone. A small dose after one drink is unlikely to be dangerous for a healthy adult, but large doses, heavy drinking, or adding prescription sedatives raise the risk. If you've been drinking, skip valerian that night.

**How long after drinking can I take valerian root?**

There's no official waiting time. A cautious rule is to wait until you're fully sober, and to skip valerian entirely on nights you've had more than a drink or two. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, but that varies widely.

**Can I drink alcohol the day after taking valerian?**

Generally yes. Valerian's effects usually wear off within several hours, so a drink the next evening is unlikely to cause a meaningful interaction for most healthy adults. If you take valerian every night or take other sedating medicines, ask your doctor or pharmacist how to plan around drinking.

**Will valerian help me sleep after drinking?**

Probably not in a useful way. Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night as your body clears it, and valerian doesn't reverse that rebound. Taking it while alcohol is still in your system mainly adds sedation and risk. Stopping drinking earlier, hydrating, and eating help more.

**Does valerian help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that valerian helps with a hangover. It doesn't address dehydration, inflammation, poor sleep, or alcohol's by-products. A warm valerian or chamomile tea the next day may feel calming, but water, food, rest, and time are what actually help.

**Can I take apigenin with alcohol?**

There's no good research on the combination. Apigenin appears to be a mild calming compound that may act on the same GABA system alcohol affects, so the cautious approach is not to take it while alcohol is still in your system. The bigger concern is a full sleep stack (valerian, apigenin, melatonin, magnesium) on top of several drinks.

**Is valerian root bad for your liver if you drink?**

Liver injury from valerian appears to be rare, but it has been reported, often with multi-ingredient products. Regular heavy drinking already strains the liver, so the combination raises the stakes for people who drink most days or have liver disease. Talk to your doctor before using valerian in those situations.

**Do valerian tinctures contain alcohol?**

Many do. Liquid valerian extracts are often made with alcohol as a solvent. The amount per dose is small, but check the label if you're avoiding alcohol for medical reasons, or choose capsules or tea instead.

**Does DHM make it safe to mix valerian and alcohol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM protects against the combined sedation of valerian and alcohol. DHM has promising early research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal studies, but it doesn't change the advice to avoid mixing sedatives with alcohol.
